```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# R prints a note when two loaded packages register the same S3 method, as
# packages loaded with robCompositions do. The note is switched off here.
Sys.setenv("_R_S3_METHOD_REGISTRATION_NOTE_OVERWRITES_" = "false")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width = "100%",
  error = FALSE
)
```

For the model engines of `comp_iv()` beyond `"lm"` and `"glm"`, the formula
interface and the diagnostics of each engine, see the four parts below.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(timecoda)
```

# The example data

To model an outcome as a function of a time-use composition, which is the
independent variable, use `comp_iv()`. For its linear and generalized linear
models, see `vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")`.

The examples use the bundled `timeuse` data. For a description of the data, see
`vignette("composition-variable", package = "timecoda")`. The data hold the
body-mass-index z-score (`zbmi`), the obesity indicator (`obesity`) and sex
(`sex`) used in the other vignettes, together with each person's school
(`school`, ten schools) and an ordered academic-achievement band (`grade`, with
the levels `below`, `expected` and `above`). They also hold the follow-up time
in months to the onset of obesity or censoring (`time`), with its event
indicator (`event`, 1 for onset).

```{r declare}
labs <- c(
  MVPA = "Moderate-to-vigorous PA",
  LPA  = "Light PA",
  SB   = "Sedentary behaviour",
  SPT  = "Sleep"
)

cd <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
  closure = 1440,
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs
)
```

# Part 1. One builder, eleven engines

Every engine is fitted by `comp_iv()` through the same procedure. The engines
differ in the effect measure reported by `summary()`, in whether `family` or
`random` must be given, and in whether a prediction on the scale of the outcome
exists. You must give `family` for `"glm"` and `"glmer"`, and the other engines
reject it. `random` is required for the clustered engines (`"coxme"`, `"lmer"`,
`"glmer"`, `"clmm"` and `"rlmer"`), optional for `"mblogit"` and rejected by the
rest.

Reallocation estimates are contrasts. For details, see
`vignette("predicting-reallocations", package = "timecoda")`.

| `model` | Backend | Use case | Effect measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"lm"` | `stats::lm()` | A continuous outcome with independent observations | mean difference |
| `"glm"` | `stats::glm()` | A binary, count or continuous outcome with a GLM family (e.g., logistic or Poisson regression) and independent observations | set by the link: odds ratio, rate, risk or mean ratio, or mean difference |
| `"cox"` | `survival::coxph()` | A time-to-event outcome with independent observations | hazard ratio |
| `"coxme"` | `coxme::coxme()` | A time-to-event outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data | hazard ratio |
| `"lmer"` | `lme4::lmer()` | A continuous outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data | mean difference |
| `"glmer"` | `lme4::glmer()` | A binary, count or continuous outcome with a GLM family and random effects for clustered or repeated data | set by the link, as for `"glm"` |
| `"clm"` | `ordinal::clm()` | An ordered-factor outcome (e.g., a graded scale) | cumulative odds ratio |
| `"clmm"` | `ordinal::clmm()` | An ordered-factor outcome with random effects for clustered or repeated data | cumulative odds ratio |
| `"mblogit"` | `mclogit::mblogit()` | An unordered-factor outcome with three or more categories, with optional random effects | relative-risk ratio, one per non-reference category |
| `"lmrob"` | `robustbase::lmrob()` | A continuous outcome with outlying observations, down-weighted by MM-estimation | mean difference |
| `"rlmer"` | `robustlmm::rlmer()` | A continuous outcome with outlying observations and random effects for clustered or repeated data | mean difference |

Five engines (`"cox"`, `"coxme"`, `"clm"`, `"clmm"` and `"mblogit"`) offer no
single scale on which to predict the outcome. On these fits,
`predict_realloc()` accepts only `type = "relative"`, its default, and `plot()`
draws only the relative surface. To draw one outcome level of a multinomial
fit, give that level to `plot()` as `category`.

The backends in the coxme, ordinal, mclogit, robustbase and robustlmm packages
are suggested packages, and `comp_iv()` checks for them when it is called. An
example that uses one of them runs only when that package is installed.

# Part 2. The engines in turn

For each family of engines, only the differences from the linear and logistic
summaries of `vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")` are
described.

## Survival outcomes: `"cox"` and `"coxme"`

```{r fit-cox}
fit_cox <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "cox", time = "time", event = "event",
                   covariates = "sex")
summary(object = fit_cox)
```

The effects are hazard ratios, and a reallocation on a Cox fit is a hazard
ratio as well. The report has no convergence line, because `comp_iv()` does not
probe Cox fits for convergence.

```{r realloc-cox}
predict_realloc(object = fit_cox, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
```

We observed that moving 10 minutes from sedentary behaviour to
moderate-to-vigorous activity was associated with a hazard of obesity onset
0.856 times that at the reference composition.

`"coxme"` extends the Cox model with random effects. To give each school a
random intercept (the term `(1 | school)`), set `random = "school"`.

```{r fit-coxme, eval = requireNamespace("coxme", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_coxme <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "coxme", time = "time",
                     event = "event", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_coxme)
```

One line is added to the summary, the median hazard ratio for school, which is
computed from the school variance `v` as `exp(sqrt(2 * v) * qnorm(0.75))`
(Austin et al., 2017). It is the median hazard ratio between two people with
identical covariates drawn from different schools, taken as the person at
higher risk over the other, and it is therefore never below 1. A value of 1
would mean no variation in hazard between schools.

## Multilevel models: `"lmer"` and `"glmer"`

```{r fit-lmer, eval = requireNamespace("pbkrtest", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_lmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmer",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_lmer)
```

We read the intraclass correlation for school, 0.264, as the share of the total
variance that lies between schools. With several grouping terms (e.g.,
`random = c("region", "school")`), one such share is reported per term.

```{r realloc-lmer, eval = requireNamespace("pbkrtest", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_lmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

The `df` column is computed with the Kenward-Roger approximation (Kenward &
Roger, 1997), which `emmeans` applies through the pbkrtest package when that
package is installed. The same method is used for the per-part rows of the
summary. For the alternatives, see the help page `?comp_iv`.

```{r fit-glmer}
fit_glmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "obesity", model = "glmer",
                     family = "binomial", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_glmer)
```

The between-school line is now a latent intraclass correlation. It is the same
share, computed on the latent scale of the logistic model with `pi^2 / 3` in
place of the residual variance (Goldstein et al., 2002). With a value of 0.001,
almost none of the variation in the odds of obesity lies between schools.

## Ordinal outcomes: `"clm"` and `"clmm"`

To fit a cumulative-link model to an ordered factor, use `"clm"`. Here the
factor is the three grade bands (`below`, `expected` and `above`, in that
order).

```{r fit-clm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_clm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clm")
summary(object = fit_clm)
```

With the parameterization of `ordinal::clm()` (Christensen, 2026), we read an
odds ratio above 1 as higher odds of a higher grade band (i.e., of being at or
above any given cut-point).

```{r fit-clmm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_clmm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clmm",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_clmm)
```

As for `"glmer"`, the latent intraclass correlation for school is computed with
`pi^2 / 3` in place of the residual variance.

## Unordered categories: `"mblogit"`

`comp_iv()` stops with an error when an ordered `grade` is given to this
engine.

To fit `"mblogit"`, add an unordered copy of `grade` to the data, with the same
levels in the same order, and declare the composition again from it.

```{r fit-mblogit, eval = requireNamespace("mclogit", quietly = TRUE)}
tu <- timeuse
tu$grade_cat <- factor(as.character(tu$grade), levels = levels(tu$grade))
cd_cat <- declare_composition(data = tu, parts = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
                              closure = 1440, units = "min/day",
                              labels = labs)

fit_mb <- comp_iv(comp = cd_cat, outcome = "grade_cat", model = "mblogit")
summary(object = fit_mb)
```

`below`, the first level, is the reference category. Each effect is a
relative-risk ratio comparing one of the other two categories with the
reference, and the new `response_level` column names the category. The omnibus
test has 6 degrees of freedom, which are three coordinates for each
non-reference category. On this fit, a reallocation also gives one row per
non-reference category.

```{r realloc-mblogit, eval = requireNamespace("mclogit", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_mb, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

To fit a clustered model with `"mblogit"`, add `random`. `random = "school"`
adds a random intercept for each school, and a bar term such as
`random = "(ilr1 | school)"` adds a random slope on a coordinate. For details,
see the help page `?comp_iv`.

## Robust linear models: `"lmrob"` and `"rlmer"`

To fit a linear model by MM-estimation (Yohai, 1987), use `"lmrob"`.

```{r fit-lmrob, eval = requireNamespace("robustbase", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_lmrob <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmrob")
summary(object = fit_lmrob)
```

To fit the robust linear mixed model (Koller, 2016), use `"rlmer"`.

```{r fit-rlmer, eval = requireNamespace("robustlmm", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_rlmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "rlmer",
                     random = "school")
summary(object = fit_rlmer)
```

Because the robustlmm package reports no degrees of freedom, every standard
error, interval and p-value of an `"rlmer"` fit is asymptotic, in the summary
and in the reallocations alike. The `df` column of a reallocation is `Inf`,
compared with 288 for the same reallocation on the `"lmer"` fit.

```{r realloc-rlmer, eval = requireNamespace("robustlmm", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_rlmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

# Part 3. The formula interface

## The `ilr()` marker

To specify the model as a formula, give `formula` in place of `outcome`,
`covariates`, `random`, `time`, `event` and `moderator`. Within it, the marker
`ilr()` stands for the whole composition. The discrete call
`outcome = "zbmi", covariates = "sex"` can be written as the formula
`zbmi ~ ilr() + sex`, and the printed fit shows the call with `ilr()` expanded.

```{r formula-main}
fit_main <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() + sex, model = "lm")
fit_main
```

Every other term is passed to the backend unchanged, so a formula can hold
interactions, random terms and transformed variables. `ilr()` is expanded by two
rules (`?ilr`).

The first rule applies inside the formula operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `:`, `/`,
`^`, `%in%`, `|` and `||` and inside parentheses. There, `ilr()` is replaced by
the sum `(ilr1 + ... + ilr(D-1))`, and R's formula algebra applies to it. In an
lme4-style engine, `(ilr() | school)` is a random slope on every coordinate.
`ilr()^2` expands to the main effects and every pairwise product of the
coordinates, with no squares.

```{r formula-sum}
fit_int <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() * sex, model = "lm")
fit_int
```

The second rule applies inside any other call, where `ilr()` is distributed.
The call is repeated once per coordinate and the copies are added, and
`I(ilr()^2)` becomes `(I(ilr1^2) + I(ilr2^2) + I(ilr3^2))`. Combining both
rules, the formula `ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2)` is the full quadratic in the
composition, with main effects, pairwise products and squares.

```{r formula-quadratic}
fit_quad <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2) + sex,
                    model = "lm")
fit_quad
```

The second rule distributes `poly(ilr(), 2)` and `splines::ns(ilr(), 3)` in the
same way. `comp_iv()` warns that the estimates may be biased when the formula
holds `ilr()` but no coordinate appears as a term of its own or as the first
argument of `poly()`, `ns()` or `bs()`.

## Moderation

To test the interaction of one covariate with the composition, name that
covariate with `moderator`. The fit is the model `zbmi ~ ilr() * sex` of
`fit_int` with the moderation test added.

```{r moderator}
fit_mod <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   moderator = "sex")
summary(object = fit_mod)
```

The moderation line reports a joint Wald test of the null hypothesis that every
composition-by-sex coefficient is zero (i.e., that the association between the
composition and z-BMI does not differ between the sexes). For each part, the
three new columns (`mod_statistic`, `mod_df` and `mod_p.value`) hold the test of
the null hypothesis that the part's own interaction with sex is zero. For
sleep, the test gives p = 0.0322, with no adjustment for the four tests.

For reallocation estimates on a fit with a composition-by-covariate
interaction, see `vignette("predicting-reallocations", package = "timecoda")`.

For a factor `moderator`, `by` defaults to the moderator when neither `by` nor
`at` names it. `fit_int`, the formula fit, is the same model, although a
formula carries no default `by`. A reallocation on `fit_int` depends on sex, and
`predict_realloc()` therefore stops with an error until you give a value for
every covariate that interacts with the composition, through `at` or `by`.

## Non-linear composition terms

```{r quadratic-summary}
summary(object = fit_quad)
```

The omnibus test now has 9 degrees of freedom, one for each coefficient that
involves only the coordinates. The curvature line reports a joint Wald test of
the null hypothesis that the coefficients of the squares and products are all
zero (i.e., that the association between the composition and z-BMI has no
curvature). Because a rotated fit with squares and products has no single
`ilr1` coefficient, each per-part row is the slope of the linear predictor in
`ilr1` at the reference composition, taken from `emmeans::emtrends()`.
`predict_realloc()` reads the quadratic fit in the same way as a linear one.

```{r quadratic-realloc}
predict_realloc(object = fit_quad, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
```

We observed that the mean z-BMI difference associated with moving 30 minutes is
less than three times that for 10 minutes.

`plot()` draws the fitted surface as one ternary panel for each group of three
parts. For this figure on a logistic fit, see
`vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")`.

```{r quadratic-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "One of four ternary panels, one for each group of three parts, of the quadratic linear model's surface of the mean difference in z-BMI from the reference composition as tiles. Several dozen small hexagonal tiles form a patch inside the triangle, coloured from dark purple for the panel's lowest mean difference to yellow for its highest, with a black point at the reference composition; the rest of the triangle is blank grey, and a legend titled Mean difference gives the scale."}
plot(x = fit_quad)
```

The full quadratic is the same model in every ILR basis, so its fit and
reallocations do not depend on the order of the parts. A squares-only
specification, `ilr() + I(ilr()^2)`, and `poly(ilr(), 2)` lack this invariance,
and their fits depend on the order of the parts given to
`declare_composition()`. For an example on `timeuse`, see the help page `?ilr`.

## The total as a covariate

The total of a composition of the waking behaviours alone (moderate-to-vigorous
activity, light activity and sedentary behaviour) varies between people. To
add this total to the model, set `include_total = TRUE`, which enters it as the
covariate `t_total` of Coenders et al. (2017), `t = sqrt(D) * log(g)`, where
`g` is the geometric mean of a person's parts on their original scale. The ILR
coefficients then give the association between the outcome and the shares of
waking time, at a constant waking time. The coefficient of `t_total` gives the
difference in the outcome associated with a longer waking day, in which every
waking behaviour is larger in the same proportion and sleep is shorter.

The waking composition is declared from the same data with three parts.
Declared with `closure = "mean"`, it is reported on the scale of the average
waking time, and the row totals before closure, shown in its summary, are the
waking times.

```{r total-data}
cd_wake <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB"),
  closure = "mean",
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs[c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB")]
)
summary(object = cd_wake, desc = FALSE, var_matrix = FALSE)
```

```{r total-fit}
fit_tot <- comp_iv(comp = cd_wake, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   include_total = TRUE)
summary(object = fit_tot)
```

The null hypothesis of the one-degree-of-freedom Wald test of `t_total` is that
its coefficient is zero (i.e., that waking time and z-BMI are not associated at
constant shares of waking time). At constant shares, a longer waking day, and so
a shorter time asleep, is associated with a higher z-BMI in these data, as the
positive coefficient shows.

```{r total-realloc}
predict_realloc(object = fit_tot, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

In a reallocation, every composition is evaluated with `t_total` held at its
reference value, the sample mean of `t_total`, and the estimate is therefore the
difference associated with the move at a constant waking time. On the
fixed-total `cd`, `include_total = TRUE` ends with an error.

# Part 4. Diagnostics per engine

The diagnostic backend used by `fit_check()` depends on the model class.

## Models checked with DHARMa

For `"lm"`, `"glm"`, `"lmer"` and `"glmer"` fits, `fit_check()` uses the DHARMa
package (Hartig, 2026). For the simulated quantile residuals, see
`vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")`. The rows reported for
a `"glmer"` fit are those of a `"glm"` fit.

## Cox models

A `"cox"` fit is checked with `survival::cox.zph()`, a test of the
proportional-hazards assumption based on the scaled Schoenfeld residuals
(Grambsch & Therneau, 1994).

```{r check-cox}
fc_cox <- fit_check(object = fit_cox, plot = FALSE)
fc_cox
```

In the global test, we found no evidence of a departure from proportional
hazards (p = 0.906). To draw the Schoenfeld residuals of each term against
time, set `plot = TRUE`.

## Ordinal models

A `"clm"` fit is checked with `ordinal::nominal_test()` (Christensen, 2026) and
with the sure package (Greenwell et al., 2018), which provides surrogate
residuals (Liu & Zhang, 2018).

```{r check-clm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("sure", quietly = TRUE)}
fc_clm <- fit_check(object = fit_clm, plot = FALSE)
fc_clm
```

In the proportional-odds tests, we found no evidence of a departure from
proportional odds for any of the three coordinates (p-values of 0.262 and
above). The surrogate residuals are random draws made under a fixed seed and
therefore repeat from call to call. To draw them, set `plot = TRUE`.

## Robust models

`"lmrob"` and `"rlmer"` fits are checked through the robustness weights of their
estimates.

```{r check-lmrob, eval = requireNamespace("robustbase", quietly = TRUE)}
fc_lmrob <- fit_check(object = fit_lmrob, plot = FALSE)
fc_lmrob
```

In this fit, the downweighted share of 0.01 corresponds to three of the 300
people, each weighted below 0.5. The rows reported for an `"rlmer"` fit are the
same.

## Engines with fit statistics only

For `"clmm"`, `"mblogit"` and `"coxme"` fits, no residual diagnostic is run, and
`fit_check()` reports the AIC and the log-likelihood with a note and draws
nothing. A `"clmm"` fit therefore has no proportional-odds test, and a
`"coxme"` fit has no proportional-hazards test. The log-likelihood of a
`"coxme"` fit is the penalized one, and the AIC uses the fit's effective degrees
of freedom.

# References

Austin, P. C., Wagner, P., & Merlo, J. (2017). The median hazard ratio: A
useful measure of variance and general contextual effects in multilevel
survival analysis. *Statistics in Medicine*, 36, 928-938.

Christensen, R. H. B. (2026). *ordinal: Regression models for ordinal data*.
R package version 2026.7-26.

Coenders, G., Martín-Fernández, J. A., & Ferrer-Rosell, B. (2017). When
relative and absolute information matter: Compositional predictor with a total
in generalized linear models. *Statistical Modelling*, 17, 494-512.

Goldstein, H., Browne, W., & Rasbash, J. (2002). Partitioning variation in
multilevel models. *Understanding Statistics*, 1, 223-231.

Grambsch, P. M., & Therneau, T. M. (1994). Proportional hazards tests and
diagnostics based on weighted residuals. *Biometrika*, 81, 515-526.

Greenwell, B. M., McCarthy, A. J., Boehmke, B. C., & Liu, D. (2018). Residuals
and diagnostics for binary and ordinal regression models: An introduction to
the sure package. *The R Journal*, 10(1).

Hartig, F. (2026). *DHARMa: Residual diagnostics for hierarchical (multi-level
/ mixed) regression models*. R package version 0.5.0.

Kenward, M. G., & Roger, J. H. (1997). Small sample inference for fixed effects
from restricted maximum likelihood. *Biometrics*, 53, 983-997.

Koller, M. (2016). robustlmm: An R package for robust estimation of linear
mixed-effects models. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 75(6), 1-24.

Liu, D., & Zhang, H. (2018). Residuals and diagnostics for ordinal regression
models: A surrogate approach. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*, 113, 845-854.

Yohai, V. J. (1987). High breakdown-point and high efficiency robust estimates
for regression. *The Annals of Statistics*, 15, 642-656.
